newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Figures for EU enlargement into eastern Europe.
newsitem.headline: Figures for EU enlargement into eastern Europe.

text.p: The European Commission presented proposals on Wednesday that it hopes will allow the European Union to admit six new countries without having to change the EU's funding system until at least 2006.
Here are the main points of the Commission's financial proposals:
-- FUTURE FINANCING: The EU will retain between 2000 and 2006 the current ceiling on how much money it spends. This is 1.27 percent of the combined Gross Domestic Product of the bloc's members.

The Commission estimates that economic growth in the bloc will be 2.5 percent a year for the current 15 EU countries and four percent in the six countries expected to start negotiations next year -- Poland, Hungary, Cyprus, Slovenia, the Czech republic, and Estonia.
That should be enough to raise the amount of money available under the ceiling by 20 billion European currency units ($22 billion) by 2006, the Commission said.
The overall EU budget would thus be 92.5 billion Ecus in 1999 rising to 111.4 billion in 2006 -- well below the ceiling, according to the Commission.

Politically, the plan would also not change the current carve up between states. Britain would continue to get its annual "money back" repayment; Germany would remain the biggest contributor, forking out 28 percent.
-- COMMON AGRICULTURAL POLICY: The Commission proposed a reform of the costly CAP -- which eats half the EU's annual budget -- to avoid an explosion caused by the newcomers and overproduction.

Guaranteed prices would be lowered by between 10 percent and 30 percent, depending on the product, with some compensation paid directly instead. The newcomers would not be fully eligible until after long transition periods of about 10 years.
Despite this, by 2006, agriculture spending is expected to rise by 7.7. billion Ecus a year because of the compensation payments, offset by just 3.7 billion Ecus from the cut in guaranteed prices.
Direct payments tied to enlargement are estimated at 1.7 billion Ecus a year at the beginning of the process, rising to 3.9 billion Ecu by the end.
-- STRUCTURAL FUNDS: Aid to the bloc's poorer countries -- about a third of the budget -- is also targeted for reform.
The goal is to keep funds at 0.46 percent of the bloc's GDP, about 275 billion Ecus over seven years, of which 45 billion will go to the eastern European countries.

Spain, Portugal, and Greece -- which currently get two-thirds of funds aimed at poorer regions -- would continue to benefit. The plan is to keep the money aimed at regions with less than 75 percent of the EU's GDP average.
As a result, Ireland -- the other main beneficiary -- would be excluded because it has become much richer.
In addition these four countries would continue to receive so-called cohesion funds -- a total of 20.5 billion Ecus over the period -- designed to improve environment and infrastructure.
